docs.title: Knowledge Base
docs.text: A running set of technical notes, organized by topic rather than by source — things learned from courses, docs, work, and debugging sessions all land in the same place, filed under the subject they belong to.

docs.title: How this is organized
docs.text:
Each topic folder has its own index.md overview plus one page per subtopic. Pages use admonitions for callouts and fenced Mermaid blocks for diagrams — no external image tool needed for most diagrams. See the root README.md for how to add a new topic or page.

This is a living document

Notes here are meant to be edited in place as understanding improves — prefer updating an existing page over letting two pages drift out of sync on the same subject.

docs.title: Software Architecture
docs.text: Structural decisions about a system: how it's decomposed into components, how those components talk to each other, and where data lives. These decisions are expensive to reverse — the pages here focus on the trade-offs behind each choice, not just the definitions.

docs.title: Pages in this topic
docs.text:
Page Covers API Design General principles that apply across REST/GraphQL/gRPC REST Resource modeling, status codes, HATEOAS GraphQL Schema design, resolvers, N+1 problem gRPC Protocol Buffers, streaming, when to prefer it over REST Microservices Service boundaries, communication, data ownership Event-Driven Architecture Pub/sub, event sourcing, CQRS

Quality attributes

Every choice on these pages trades off against scalability, availability, latency, consistency, and maintainability. There's no universally "best" answer — only the right trade-off for a given system's actual requirements.

docs.title: What is the CAP Theorem?
docs.text:
The CAP Theorem, proposed by Eric Brewer, states:

A distributed database cannot simultaneously guarantee Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance when a network partition occurs.

When the network is healthy, a system may provide all three. The trade-off happens during a network partition.

docs.text:
Instead of one database server:

Database

Example:

Database A

XXXXXXXX Network Failure XXXXXXXX

Database B

The databases cannot communicate, but the system continues to function.

docs.text:

docs.title: CP Systems
docs.text:
Prioritize:

  • Consistency
  • Partition Tolerance

May reject requests during network failures.

Examples:

  • HBase
  • ZooKeeper
  • etcd

Best for:

  • Banking
  • Payment systems
  • Inventory management

docs.title: AP Systems
docs.text:
Prioritize:

  • Availability
  • Partition Tolerance

May temporarily return stale data.

Examples:

  • Cassandra
  • Riak
  • DynamoDB (configurable)

Best for:

  • Social media
  • Chat applications
  • Product catalogs
  • News feeds

docs.title: CA Systems
docs.text:
CA means:

  • Consistency
  • Availability

Without partition tolerance.

Example:

Client

↓

Single Database Server

Traditional relational databases (like MySQL or PostgreSQL on a single server) behave like CA because there is no distributed network between database nodes.

However, in real distributed environments, network partitions are always possible, so pure CA systems are generally not practical.

docs.title: CAP Summary
docs.text: Property Meaning Consistency Every client sees the latest data. Availability Every request receives a response. Partition Tolerance The system continues operating despite network failures.

docs.title: CP vs AP
docs.text: CP AP Always returns consistent data Always returns a response May reject requests May return stale data Better for financial systems Better for high-traffic web systems

docs.title: Banking (CP)
docs.text:
Transfer $100

↓

Must update every database correctly

↓

If synchronization fails

↓

Reject transaction

Correctness is more important than availability.

docs.title: Social Media (AP)
docs.text:
User changes profile picture

↓

Some users see old picture

↓

Others see new picture

↓

Eventually everyone sees new picture

Temporary inconsistency is acceptable.

docs.title: Popular Databases
docs.text: Database CAP Preference MySQL (single server) CA PostgreSQL (single server) CA MongoDB CP (default replica set behavior) Cassandra AP Riak AP HBase CP ZooKeeper CP etcd CP

docs.title: Q1. What is the CAP Theorem?
docs.text:
Answer

The CAP Theorem states that during a network partition, a distributed system can guarantee at most two of the following three properties: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance.

docs.title: Q2. What is Consistency?
docs.text:
Answer

Every client sees the same, most recent committed data.

docs.title: Q3. What is Availability?
docs.text:
Answer

Every request receives a response, even if some servers have failed.

docs.title: Q4. What is Partition Tolerance?
docs.text:
Answer

The system continues operating even when communication between distributed nodes is interrupted.

docs.title: Q5. Why is Partition Tolerance important?
docs.text:
Answer

Because network failures are unavoidable in distributed systems. A distributed database must continue operating despite communication problems.

docs.title: Q6. What is the difference between CP and AP?
docs.text:
Answer

  • CP prioritizes consistency over availability during a partition.
  • AP prioritizes availability over strong consistency during a partition.

docs.title: Q7. Which applications should choose CP?
docs.text:
Answer

Applications where correctness is critical, such as banking, payment processing, and inventory systems.

docs.title: Q8. Which applications should choose AP?
docs.text:
Answer

Applications where high availability is more important than immediate consistency, such as social media, chat systems, and news feeds.

docs.title: What is a CDN?
docs.text:
A Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a globally distributed network of edge servers that cache content closer to users.

Instead of every request going to the origin server, users are served by the nearest CDN edge server whenever possible.

Benefits:

  • Faster page loading
  • Lower latency
  • Reduced origin server load
  • Better scalability
  • Improved availability

docs.title: Without CDN
docs.text:
User (Japan)
                  |
                  |
           Long Distance
                  |
                  |
          Origin Server (US)

Problems:

  • High latency
  • Slow loading
  • Heavy load on origin server

docs.title: With CDN
docs.text:
User (Japan)
                     |
             Nearby Edge Server
                     |
             (Cached Content)
                     |
      Only if cache miss/stale
                     |
              Origin Server (US)

The user gets content from the closest edge server.

docs.title: 1. Pull CDN
docs.text:
The CDN automatically fetches content from the origin server when needed.

Example:

Client

↓

CDN

↓

Image not cached

↓

Origin Server

↓

Return image

↓

Store in CDN

docs.title: TTL (Time To Live)
docs.text:
The CDN keeps cached content for a configured time.

Example:

TTL = 1 hour

12:00

↓

Image cached

↓

1:00 PM

↓

Cache expires

Important: After the TTL expires, the CDN typically does not immediately contact the origin. Instead, the next client request triggers the CDN to fetch a fresh copy from the origin.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Easy to set up
  • Minimal maintenance
  • Automatically caches requested content

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• First request after expiration is slower
  • Users may temporarily receive stale content depending on cache settings

docs.title: 2. Push CDN
docs.text:
The origin server uploads content to the CDN whenever content changes.

Example:

Origin Server

↓

Upload image

↓

CDN

↓

Edge Servers

Client requests:

Client

↓

CDN

↓

Return cached image

The CDN does not need to fetch from the origin because the content was already pushed.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Content is immediately available on the CDN
  • Better control over cached content
  • Good for predictable static assets

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• More complex deployment
  • Need synchronization/upload logic
  • More storage management

docs.title: Static Content
docs.text:
Best suited for CDNs.

Examples:

  • Images
  • CSS
  • JavaScript
  • Videos
  • PDFs
  • Fonts

docs.title: Dynamic Content
docs.text:
Usually comes from the origin server.

Examples:

  • Login
  • Bank transfer
  • Shopping cart
  • User profile

Some modern CDNs can accelerate dynamic content, but they generally don't cache personalized responses by default.

docs.title: Popular CDN Providers
docs.text:
• Cloudflare
  • Amazon CloudFront
  • Akamai
  • Fastly
  • Google Cloud CDN
  • Azure CDN

docs.title: Advantages of CDN
docs.text:
• Faster page loading
  • Lower latency
  • Reduced bandwidth usage
  • Reduced origin server load
  • Better scalability
  • Improved availability
  • Protection against traffic spikes
  • Can help mitigate DDoS attacks (depending on the provider)

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
• Dynamic data is usually not cached.
  • Choose an appropriate TTL.
  • Update or invalidate the cache when content changes.
  • CDN is not a replacement for your origin server.

docs.title: Q1. What is a CDN?
docs.text:
Answer

A CDN is a distributed network of edge servers that caches content closer to users to reduce latency and improve performance.

docs.title: Q2. Why do we use a CDN?
docs.text:
Answer

To reduce latency, improve page loading speed, reduce origin server load, increase scalability, and improve availability.

docs.title: Q3. What is the difference between Pull CDN and Push CDN?
docs.text: Pull CDN Push CDN CDN fetches content when needed Origin uploads content to CDN Easy to configure More complex setup First request may be slower Content is immediately available Good for most websites Good for controlled static assets

docs.title: Q4. What is TTL?
docs.text:
Answer

TTL (Time To Live) defines how long the CDN keeps cached content before considering it stale and needing a fresh copy from the origin.

docs.title: Q5. What is a Cache Hit?
docs.text:
Answer

The requested content already exists in the CDN cache, so it can be returned immediately without contacting the origin server.

docs.title: Q6. What is a Cache Miss?
docs.text:
Answer

The content is not in the CDN cache (or the cache is stale), so the CDN retrieves it from the origin server, stores it, and then returns it to the client.

docs.title: Q7. Can a CDN cache API responses?
docs.text:
Answer

Yes, if the API responses are cacheable (for example, public product catalogs or news articles). Personalized or sensitive responses are usually not cached.

docs.title: What is Unstructured Data?
docs.text:
Unstructured data is data that does not fit well into rows and columns.

Examples:

  • Images
  • Videos
  • Audio files
  • PDF documents
  • Office files
  • Backups
  • Machine learning models

Unlike relational data, it does not have a fixed schema.

docs.title: Semi-Structured
docs.text:
{
  "name": "Alice",
  "age": 22,
  "skills": [
    "Java",
    "Spring"
  ]
}

Example:

  • MongoDB
  • CouchDB

docs.title: Unstructured
docs.text:
photo.jpg

video.mp4

report.pdf

music.mp3

Usually stored as binary files.

docs.text:
BLOB stands for Binary Large Object.

A BLOB is binary data stored as a single object.

Examples:

docs.title: Q1. What is unstructured data?
docs.text:
Answer

Unstructured data is data without a predefined tabular schema, such as images, videos, PDFs, and audio files.

docs.title: Q2. What does BLOB stand for?
docs.text:
Answer

Binary Large Object—a binary file stored as a single object.

docs.title: Q3. Should we store images directly in a relational database?
docs.text:
Answer

Usually no.

Large files are typically stored in object storage, while the database stores metadata such as the file name or URL.

docs.title: Q4. What is Object Storage?
docs.text:
Answer

Object storage stores files as independent objects together with metadata. It is highly scalable and designed for storing large amounts of unstructured data.

docs.title: Q5. What should be stored in MySQL and what should be stored in Amazon S3?
docs.text:
Answer

Store structured metadata (user ID, filename, URL, upload time) in MySQL, and store the actual binary file (image, video, PDF) in Amazon S3.

docs.title: Q6. What is the difference between MongoDB and Amazon S3?
docs.text: MongoDB Amazon S3 Stores JSON-like documents Stores binary objects/files Query document fields Retrieve objects by key Semi-structured data Unstructured file storage

docs.title: What is an API Gateway?
docs.text:
An API Gateway is the single entry point for clients to access backend services.

Instead of clients calling each microservice directly, they send requests to the gateway, which forwards them to the appropriate service.

docs.title: Without API Gateway
docs.text:
Client
              /    |     \
             /     |      \
            /      |       \
      User API  Order API  Payment API

Problems:

  • Client must know every service.
  • More network calls.
  • Authentication implemented in multiple services.
  • Hard to modify service addresses.
  • Harder to monitor traffic.

docs.title: With API Gateway
docs.text:
Client
                   |
          +----------------+
          | API Gateway    |
          +----------------+
            /      |      \
           /       |       \
      User API  Order API  Payment API

The client only communicates with the gateway.

docs.title: Why do we need an API Gateway?
docs.text:
In a microservices architecture, there may be dozens or even hundreds of services.

Without a gateway:

  • Clients must know every endpoint.
  • Authentication is duplicated.
  • Routing logic is spread across clients.
  • Service changes affect clients.

The API Gateway solves these problems by acting as a single entry point.

docs.title: 1. Request Routing
docs.text:
GET /orders

↓

API Gateway

↓

Order Service

The gateway forwards requests to the correct service.

docs.title: 2. Authentication & Authorization
docs.text:
Client

↓

JWT Token

↓

API Gateway

↓

Validate Token

↓

Forward Request

Instead of every service validating JWTs, the gateway can perform the initial authentication and authorization.

docs.title: 3. Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Prevent abuse by limiting requests.

Client

↓

1000 requests/sec ❌

↓

Gateway

↓

100 requests/sec ✅

docs.title: 4. Load Balancing
docs.text:
The gateway can distribute requests across multiple instances of the same service.

Gateway

↓

Order Service A

Order Service B

Order Service C

docs.title: 5. Response Caching
docs.text:
Frequently requested data can be cached.

Client

↓

Gateway Cache

↓

If found → Return immediately

Else → Call backend

Benefits:

  • Faster responses
  • Reduced backend load

docs.title: 6. Logging & Monitoring
docs.text:
The gateway records:

  • Request count
  • Response time
  • Error rate
  • User activity

This helps with monitoring and troubleshooting.

docs.title: 7. SSL/TLS Termination
docs.text:
HTTPS connections can end at the gateway.

HTTPS

↓

Gateway

↓

HTTP (internal network)

This reduces encryption overhead on backend services while keeping external communication secure.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Single entry point for clients
  • Simplifies client applications
  • Centralizes authentication and authorization
  • Supports rate limiting
  • Supports response caching
  • Provides monitoring and logging
  • Enables seamless backend changes
  • Hides internal services from external users
  • Works with services written in different languages

docs.title: Do NOT put business logic in the gateway.
docs.text:
Good:

  • Authentication
  • Routing
  • Caching
  • Rate limiting

Bad:

  • Calculate discounts
  • Process payments
  • Create orders

Business logic belongs in backend services.

docs.title: Single Point of Failure
docs.text:
One gateway instance is risky.

Production deployment:

             Client
                |
        Load Balancer
           /       \
          /         \
 Gateway A       Gateway B
      |               |
   Microservices

Deploy multiple gateway instances behind a load balancer.

docs.title: Prevent Gateway Bypass
docs.text:
Good:

Internet

↓

API Gateway

↓

Microservices

Bad:

Internet

↓

Order Service

Backend services should only be accessible internally.

docs.title: API Gateway vs Load Balancer
docs.text:
API Gateway Load Balancer Routes based on API paths Distributes traffic Authentication No authentication (typically) Rate limiting No Caching Usually no Logging Basic Business-aware routing No Works at application layer (L7) Often Layer 4 or Layer 7

A gateway often includes load-balancing capabilities, but a load balancer is not a full API Gateway.

docs.title: Common API Gateway Products
docs.text:
• Kong
  • NGINX
  • Spring Cloud Gateway
  • Envoy
  • AWS API Gateway
  • Azure API Management
  • Apigee

docs.title: Q1. What is an API Gateway?
docs.text:
Answer

An API Gateway is the single entry point for client requests. It routes requests to backend services and handles cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, rate limiting, caching, and logging.

docs.title: Q2. Why do we need an API Gateway?
docs.text:
Answer

To simplify client communication, centralize common functionality, improve security, and hide the internal microservice architecture.

docs.title: Q3. Should an API Gateway contain business logic?
docs.text:
Answer

No.

It should only handle infrastructure concerns such as routing, authentication, caching, logging, and rate limiting. Business logic belongs in backend services.

docs.title: Q4. Is an API Gateway a Single Point of Failure?
docs.text:
Answer

It can be.

In production, multiple gateway instances are deployed behind a load balancer for high availability.

docs.title: Q5. What's the difference between an API Gateway and a Load Balancer?
docs.text:
Answer

A load balancer mainly distributes traffic across service instances.

An API Gateway provides additional features such as authentication, authorization, routing, caching, rate limiting, logging, and API aggregation.

docs.title: Q6. Can clients directly call microservices?
docs.text:
Answer

Generally, no.

External clients should access services only through the API Gateway to enforce security and maintain a consistent API surface.

docs.title: Q7. Can an API Gateway communicate with services written in different programming languages?
docs.text:
Answer

Yes.

As long as services expose standard protocols such as HTTP or gRPC, the gateway can route requests regardless of the implementation language.

docs.title: API Design Principles
docs.text: Principles that hold regardless of which protocol (REST/GraphQL/gRPC) sits on top.

docs.title: Design for the consumer, not the database
docs.text: An API's shape should reflect how clients need to use the data, not how it's stored internally. Leaking internal schema details into the API contract makes both sides harder to evolve independently.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
• URI versioning (/v1/orders) — simple, visible, but can lead to duplicated logic across versions.
  • Header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json) — keeps URLs clean, less discoverable.
  • Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes (new optional fields) over bumping a version at all, when possible.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text: Any operation that might be retried (network blip, client timeout) should be safe to run twice. PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST typically isn't — use an idempotency key header for POST endpoints that create resources, so a retried request doesn't create a duplicate.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
Prefer cursor-based over offset-based at scale

OFFSET 100000 forces the database to scan and discard 100,000 rows. A cursor (?after=<opaque-id>) lets the database jump straight to the right position and stays correct even if rows are inserted/deleted mid-pagination.

docs.title: Error responses
docs.text:
Return structured, machine-parseable errors — a stable code, a human-readable message, and enough context to act on it:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",
    "message": "email must be a valid address",
    "field": "email"
  }
}

docs.title: Event-Driven Architecture
docs.text: Components communicate by producing and reacting to events instead of calling each other directly, decoupling producers from consumers in both time and identity.

docs.title: Queues vs topics
docs.text: Queue (point-to-point) Topic (pub/sub) Delivery One consumer per message Every subscriber gets the message Use case Distributing work across a worker pool Broadcasting a fact ("order placed")

docs.title: Delivery guarantees
docs.text:
• At-most-once — may lose messages, never duplicates. Fine for data you can afford to drop (some metrics).
  • At-least-once — never loses messages, may duplicate. The common default — requires idempotent consumers.
  • Exactly-once — the ideal; in practice approximated via at-least-once
  • deduplication (idempotency keys), rather than a true guarantee.

docs.title: Event sourcing
docs.text:
Store every state change as an immutable event instead of just the current state. Current state is derived by replaying events from the beginning (or from a snapshot).

graph LR
    E1[AccountOpened] --> E2[Deposited $100]
    E2 --> E3[Withdrew $30]
    E3 --> S["Current state: balance = $70<br/>(derived by replay)"]

Benefits: full audit trail, ability to reconstruct state at any point in time, natural fit with event-driven systems. Cost: more moving parts than just storing current state, and querying "current state" directly requires either replay-on-read or a materialized view.

docs.title: CQRS
docs.text:
Command Query Responsibility Segregation — separate the write model (handles commands, often event-sourced) from the read model (denormalized views optimized for specific queries, built from those events). Useful when read and write patterns have very different scaling needs — e.g. rare complex writes, frequent simple reads.

Tip

Event sourcing and CQRS are often taught together but are independent — you can use CQRS with a normal database, and event sourcing without CQRS. Reach for both together only when the combined complexity is actually justified by the read/write asymmetry.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text: A query language for APIs where the client specifies exactly what shape of data it needs, and the server resolves it from one or more sources in a single round trip.

docs.title: Schema-first design
docs.text:
Everything starts from a strongly-typed schema (SDL):

type Order {
  id: ID!
  status: OrderStatus!
  items: [OrderItem!]!
  customer: Customer!
}

type Query {
  order(id: ID!): Order
}

The schema is the contract — clients can introspect it to know exactly what's available, which tooling (autocomplete, codegen) relies on heavily.

docs.title: Resolvers
docs.text: Each field has a resolver function that knows how to fetch its value, independent of other fields. This is GraphQL's core trade-off: flexibility for the client, complexity pushed to the server to resolve an arbitrary combination of fields efficiently.

docs.title: The N+1 problem
docs.text:
Naively resolving Order.customer for a list of 100 orders triggers 100 separate customer lookups (one per order) on top of the 1 query for the orders themselves — 101 queries total.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    participant DB as Database
    C->>S: query { orders { id customer { name } } }
    S->>DB: SELECT * FROM orders
    loop for each order
        S->>DB: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = ?
    end

Fix: batch and cache lookups within a single request using a DataLoader pattern — collect all the customer IDs needed across the request, then issue one WHERE id IN (...) query.

docs.title: Trade-offs vs REST
docs.text: REST GraphQL Over/under-fetching Common (fixed response shape) Client controls exact shape Caching Simple (HTTP caching by URL) Harder (single endpoint, POST-based) Learning curve Low Higher (schema, resolvers, N+1 awareness) Best fit Simple CRUD, public APIs Complex/nested data, many client shapes (mobile vs web)

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text: A binary RPC framework built on HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers, designed for fast, strongly-typed service-to-service communication.

docs.title: Protocol Buffers
docs.text:
Contracts are defined in .proto files and compiled into client/server code for many languages — the schema is enforced at compile time, not discovered at runtime like a JSON API:

service OrderService {
  rpc GetOrder (OrderRequest) returns (OrderResponse);
  rpc StreamOrders (OrderFilter) returns (stream OrderResponse);
}

message OrderRequest {
  string order_id = 1;
}

Binary encoding is smaller and faster to (de)serialize than JSON — a real win at high request volume between internal services.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
Beyond simple request/response, gRPC supports:

  • Server streaming — one request, a stream of responses (e.g. live price updates).
  • Client streaming — a stream of requests, one response (e.g. uploading chunks).
  • Bidirectional streaming — both sides stream independently (e.g. a chat connection).

docs.title: When to prefer gRPC over REST
docs.text:
Favor gRPC when Favor REST when Internal service-to-service calls Public-facing APIs (browser clients, third parties) Need streaming Simple request/response is enough Performance/latency is critical Human-readable payloads matter for debugging Polyglot microservices with shared .proto contracts Ecosystem/tooling maturity for REST is a requirement

Note

Browsers can't call gRPC directly without a proxy (gRPC-Web) — this is the main reason gRPC dominates internal service meshes but REST/GraphQL still dominate public and browser-facing APIs.

docs.title: What is Load Balancing?
docs.text:
Load balancing is the process of distributing incoming client requests across multiple servers so that no single server becomes overloaded.

Without a load balancer:

                1000 Requests
                     |
                  Server A
             CPU = 100% ❌

With a load balancer:

                1000 Requests
                     |
              +----------------+
              | Load Balancer  |
              +----------------+
               /      |       \
              /       |        \
        Server A  Server B  Server C
          30%       35%       35%

docs.title: Why do we need Load Balancing?
docs.text:
When a system scales horizontally, we run multiple servers instead of one powerful server.

Instead of every client choosing a server, a load balancer acts as the coordinator and forwards each request to an appropriate server.

Benefits:

  • Prevents one server from becoming overloaded
  • Improves system performance
  • Enables horizontal scaling
  • Increases availability
  • Supports fault tolerance
  • Makes maintenance easier (servers can be updated one at a time)

docs.title: Horizontal Scaling
docs.text:
Instead of

Client
  |
Server (8 CPU)

we scale like this:

                Clients
                   |
           +----------------+
           | Load Balancer  |
           +----------------+
             /     |      \
            /      |       \
       Server1 Server2 Server3

docs.title: 1. DNS Load Balancing
docs.text:
How it works:

Client
   |
DNS Query
   |
DNS Server
   |
Returns one IP address

Example:
example.com
↓

192.168.1.10

Sometimes DNS rotates the returned IP:

Request 1 -> Server A
Request 2 -> Server B
Request 3 -> Server C

This is called Round Robin DNS.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Very simple
  • Cheap
  • No extra infrastructure

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Cannot accurately detect unhealthy servers
  • DNS caching means users may continue using a dead server
  • Cannot make intelligent routing decisions
  • Cannot consider server CPU or memory usage

docs.title: 2. Hardware Load Balancer
docs.text:
A dedicated physical appliance.

Example:

              Clients
                  |
         Hardware Load Balancer
                  |
      +-----------+-----------+
      |           |           |
   Server A    Server B    Server C

Examples:

  • F5 BIG-IP
  • Citrix ADC

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Very high performance
  • Reliable
  • Excellent health checking
  • Advanced routing

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Expensive
  • Requires dedicated hardware
  • Harder to scale than software solutions

docs.title: 3. Software Load Balancer
docs.text:
Software running on a VM, server, or container.

Examples:

  • Nginx
  • HAProxy
  • Envoy
  • Traefik

Architecture:

              Clients
                  |
          Nginx / HAProxy
                  |
      +-----------+-----------+
      |           |           |
   Server A    Server B    Server C

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Low cost
  • Easy to configure
  • Easy to scale
  • Supports health checks
  • Flexible

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Still consumes CPU/RAM on the machine it runs on
  • Usually less powerful than high-end hardware appliances

Note:

A software load balancer still runs on a machine (physical server, VM, or container). It does not magically work without compute resources.

docs.title: 4. Global Server Load Balancer (GSLB)
docs.text:
Used when servers are located in multiple geographic regions.

Example:

                 User

                  |
              GSLB (DNS)

      +-----------+-----------+
      |                       |
  US Datacenter          Asia Datacenter
      |                       |
   Load Balancer          Load Balancer
      |                       |
 Servers...               Servers...

The GSLB chooses the best region based on:

  • User location
  • Latency
  • Server health
  • Capacity
  • Policies

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Supports worldwide users
  • High availability
  • Disaster recovery
  • Routes users to the nearest healthy region

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• More complex
  • More expensive
  • Usually cloud or enterprise solutions

Examples:

  • AWS Route 53
  • Azure Traffic Manager
  • Cloudflare Load Balancing

docs.title: Round Robin
docs.text:
Req1 -> A
Req2 -> B
Req3 -> C
Req4 -> A

Simple but ignores server capacity.

docs.title: Weighted Round Robin
docs.text:
Server A Weight = 5
Server B Weight = 2
Server C Weight = 1

Requests:

A A A A A B B C

Powerful servers receive more requests.

docs.title: Least Connections
docs.text:
Send new requests to the server with the fewest active connections.

Example:

Server A : 100 connections

Server B : 20 connections

Server C : 15 connections

↓

Next request → Server C

docs.title: IP Hash
docs.text:
The client's IP determines which server is selected.

Useful when a user should consistently reach the same server.

docs.title: Health Check
docs.text:
A load balancer periodically checks whether servers are healthy.

Load Balancer

↓

GET /health

↓

Server A → 200 OK ✅

Server B → Timeout ❌

↓

Do not send requests to Server B

docs.title: Q1. Why do we need a load balancer?
docs.text:
Answer

To distribute incoming requests across multiple servers, preventing overload, improving performance, increasing availability, enabling horizontal scaling, and simplifying maintenance.

docs.title: Q2. What is horizontal scaling?
docs.text:
Answer

Horizontal scaling means adding more servers instead of increasing the power of a single server.

docs.title: Q3. What's the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
docs.text:
Answer

Vertical scaling increases the resources (CPU, RAM) of one server.

Horizontal scaling adds more servers.

docs.title: Q4. Does DNS load balancing know whether a server is down?
docs.text:
Answer

Not by itself.

Traditional Round Robin DNS simply rotates IP addresses and cannot accurately detect server health. Because of DNS caching, clients may still connect to an unavailable server.

docs.title: Q5. Can software load balancers perform health checks?
docs.text:
Answer

Yes.

Modern software load balancers like Nginx and HAProxy can periodically check backend server health.

docs.title: Q6. What is the difference between a hardware and software load balancer?
docs.text: Hardware Software Dedicated appliance Runs on a server/VM/container Expensive Low cost Very high performance Flexible and scalable Enterprise data centers Most cloud-native applications

docs.title: Q7. What is GSLB?
docs.text:
Answer

Global Server Load Balancing distributes users across multiple regions or data centers based on latency, health, location, or routing policies.

docs.title: Q8. Which load balancing algorithm should be used if servers have different capacities?
docs.text:
Answer

Weighted Round Robin.

More powerful servers receive a larger share of traffic.

docs.title: Q9. Which algorithm works best when requests have long-lived connections?
docs.text:
Answer

Least Connections.

It balances based on the number of active connections rather than simply counting requests.

docs.title: Q10. Is a load balancer a single point of failure?
docs.text:
Answer

It can be.

In production, organizations often deploy multiple load balancers with failover mechanisms (active-active or active-passive) to avoid a single point of failure.

docs.title: What is a Message Broker?
docs.text:
A Message Broker is middleware that sits between producers and consumers.

Instead of services communicating directly, they exchange messages through the broker.

Examples:

  • RabbitMQ
  • Apache Kafka
  • ActiveMQ
  • Amazon SQS
  • Google Pub/Sub

docs.title: Why do we need a Message Broker?
docs.text:
Imagine an e-commerce system.

Without a message broker:

Client
   |
Order Service
   |
   +--> Payment Service
   |
   +--> Inventory Service
   |
   +--> Email Service
   |
   +--> Analytics Service

Client waits until ALL services finish.

Problems:

  • Slow response
  • Tight coupling
  • One failed service may affect others
  • Difficult to scale

With a message broker:

                 Client
                    |
             Order Service
                    |
          Save Order in Database
                    |
          Publish Message
                    |
          +------------------+
          | Message Broker   |
          +------------------+
           /       |        \
          /        |         \
 Payment   Inventory   Email Service
 Service     Service

The client receives a response immediately after the order is accepted.

Other services continue working in the background.

docs.title: Producer and Consumer
docs.text:
Producer

↓

Message Broker

↓

Consumer

Producer:

  • Sends messages

Consumer:

  • Reads messages and processes them

docs.title: 1. Asynchronous Processing
docs.text:
Instead of waiting for every task:

Client
   |
Order Service
   |
Return Success

Background:

Broker
   |
Email
Inventory
Analytics

The client gets a response much sooner.

docs.title: 2. Decoupling Services
docs.text:
Without broker:

Order Service

↓

Email Service

Order Service must know Email Service's address.

With broker:

Order Service

↓

Broker

↓

Email Service

Neither service needs direct knowledge of the other.

docs.title: 3. Buffering Traffic
docs.text:
Suppose:

100,000 orders arrive in one minute.

Email service can only process:

1,000 emails/minute.

Broker queue:

100000 Messages

↓

Queue

↓

Email Service

The queue stores messages until consumers are ready.

docs.title: 4. Reliability
docs.text:
Modern brokers can:

  • Store messages persistently
  • Retry failed deliveries
  • Require acknowledgements (ACKs)
  • Prevent message loss during temporary failures

docs.title: 5. Scalability
docs.text:
One consumer:

Queue

↓

Consumer A

Many consumers:

Queue

↓

Consumer A

Consumer B

Consumer C

Messages are distributed among consumers.

docs.title: Does a Message Broker Reduce Latency?
docs.text:
This is a common interview question.

Answer: Not exactly.

Example:

Without broker:

Client

↓

Create Order

↓

Payment (2s)

↓

Email (3s)

↓

Inventory (1s)

↓

Return Response

Total = 6 seconds

With broker:

Client

↓

Create Order

↓

Save Order

↓

Publish Message (20 ms)

↓

Return Response

Total ≈ 100–200 ms

Background:

Payment
Inventory
Email

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
The overall work is not finished sooner.

Instead:

  • The client experiences lower response time.
  • Background tasks continue asynchronously.

So a message broker improves perceived latency (user response time), not necessarily the total processing time.

docs.title: Message Queue Example
docs.text:
Producer

↓

+--------------------+
| Order Created      |
| Order Created      |
| Order Created      |
+--------------------+

↓

Consumer

Messages wait until a consumer processes them.

docs.title: Common Use Cases
docs.text:
• Sending emails
  • SMS notifications
  • Image processing
  • Video transcoding
  • Payment events
  • Order processing
  • Logging
  • Analytics
  • Event-driven microservices

docs.title: Popular Message Brokers
docs.text: Broker Best For RabbitMQ General messaging, task queues Apache Kafka High-throughput event streaming ActiveMQ Enterprise Java applications Amazon SQS AWS cloud messaging Google Pub/Sub GCP event systems

docs.title: Q1. What is a Message Broker?
docs.text:
Answer

Middleware that enables producers and consumers to communicate asynchronously by exchanging messages.

docs.title: Q2. Why do we use a Message Broker?
docs.text:
Answer

To enable asynchronous processing, decouple services, buffer traffic, improve reliability, and scale systems more easily.

docs.title: Q3. Does a Message Broker make processing faster?
docs.text:
Answer

Not necessarily.

It usually reduces the client's waiting time, while the actual work continues in the background.

docs.title: Q4. Can messages be lost?
docs.text:
Answer

They can be if the broker is configured without durability or acknowledgements. Production systems use features such as persistent storage, ACKs, and retries to minimize message loss.

docs.title: Q5. What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous communication?
Synchronous
docs.text:
Client

↓

Wait

↓

Response

The client waits until the work is completed.

docs.title: Asynchronous
docs.text:
Client

↓

Accepted

↓

Continue working

Background processing...

The client does not wait for all background tasks to finish.

docs.title: Q6. Why is a queue useful during traffic spikes?
docs.text:
Answer

The queue buffers incoming messages so producers can continue sending requests while consumers process them at their own pace, preventing overload.

docs.title: Q7. Can multiple consumers process the same queue?
docs.text:
Answer

Yes.

Multiple consumers can share a queue, allowing messages to be processed in parallel and increasing throughput.

docs.title: Microservices
docs.text: Independently deployable services, each owning its own data, communicating over the network instead of in-process function calls.

docs.title: Finding service boundaries
docs.text: The most reliable heuristic is Domain-Driven Design's bounded context — split along areas of the business where a term means one specific thing. Splitting by technical layer (a "database service") is a common mistake: it creates services that always change together, which is worse than a monolith with none of the benefits of either approach.

docs.title: Communication patterns
docs.text:
graph LR
    C[Client] --> GW[API Gateway]
    GW --> A[Orders Service]
    GW --> B[Users Service]
    A -- async event --> Q[(Message Broker)]
    Q --> D[Billing Service]
    Q --> E[Notifications Service]
  • Synchronous (REST/gRPC) — simple, immediate response, but couples the caller's availability to the callee's.
  • Asynchronous (events/queues) — decoupled, more resilient to downstream slowness, harder to trace end-to-end.

docs.title: Data ownership
docs.text: Each service owns its database exclusively — no other service queries it directly. Cross-service data needs go through the owning service's API or via events, never a shared database table.

docs.title: Distributed transactions: sagas
docs.text:
No cross-service ACID transaction is possible once each service has its own database. A saga breaks a business transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo it on failure:

  1. Reserve inventory
  2. Charge payment

  3. If charge fails → release inventory (compensating action)

  4. Orchestrated — a central coordinator drives each step explicitly.

  5. Choreographed — each service reacts to the previous step's event; no central coordinator, but harder to see the overall flow.

Microservices aren't free

They trade development-time simplicity for operational complexity: distributed tracing, service discovery, network failure handling, and eventual consistency all become the team's problem. Worth it when org size or independent-scaling needs justify it — not a default.

docs.title: What is a NoSQL Database?
docs.text:
A NoSQL (Not Only SQL) database stores data using non-relational data models instead of tables with fixed schemas.

Unlike relational databases, NoSQL databases are designed for:

  • Flexible schemas
  • Horizontal scalability
  • High availability
  • High read/write throughput
  • Large volumes of semi-structured or unstructured data

Popular NoSQL databases:

  • MongoDB
  • Redis
  • Cassandra
  • DynamoDB
  • Neo4j

docs.title: Relational Database (SQL)
docs.text:
Data is stored in tables with relationships.

Users
+----+-------+
| id | name  |
+----+-------+

Orders
+---------+---------+
| orderId | userId  |
+---------+---------+

JOIN

Characteristics:

  • Fixed schema
  • Foreign keys
  • JOIN operations
  • ACID transactions

docs.title: NoSQL Database
docs.text:
Data is stored using different models.

Key-Value
Document
Graph

Characteristics:

  • Flexible schema
  • Easy horizontal scaling
  • Optimized for specific use cases
  • Usually avoids expensive JOIN operations

docs.title: When to use NoSQL
docs.text:
Use NoSQL when:

  • Data structure changes frequently.
  • The application needs to scale horizontally.
  • High read/write performance is required.
  • The application stores JSON-like or hierarchical data.
  • Relationships between data are simple or can be embedded.

Examples:

  • Social media
  • Chat applications
  • Product catalogs
  • IoT
  • Logging systems
  • Recommendation systems

docs.title: 1. Key-Value Database
docs.text:
Stores data as a key and its associated value.

"user:1"

↓

{
   "name":"Alice",
   "age":22
}

Similar to:

Map<String, Object>

Examples:

  • Redis
  • Amazon DynamoDB
  • Riak

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Extremely fast
  • Simple data model
  • Excellent for caching

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Cache
  • Session storage
  • Shopping carts
  • Authentication tokens

docs.title: 2. Document Database
docs.text:
Stores collections of documents.

Each document is a self-contained object (usually JSON/BSON) representing one entity.

Example:

{
  "_id": 1,
  "name": "Alice",
  "age": 22,
  "address": {
    "city": "Hanoi"
  },
  "orders": [
    {
      "id": 101,
      "price": 100
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Stores collections of documents.
  • Each document is an object.
  • Different documents can have different attributes.
  • Attributes can have different data types.
  • Supports nested objects and arrays.
  • Documents map naturally to programming language objects.

Example:

Java Object

class User {
    String name;
    int age;
    Address address;
    List<Order> orders;
}

↓

MongoDB Document

{
  "name": "Alice",
  "age": 22,
  "address": { ... },
  "orders": [ ... ]
}

Examples:

  • MongoDB
  • CouchDB
  • Firebase Firestore

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Flexible schema
  • Easy object mapping
  • Great for APIs returning JSON
  • Supports nested data naturally

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• User profiles
  • Product catalogs
  • CMS
  • Mobile applications

docs.title: 3. Graph Database
docs.text:
Optimized for navigating and analyzing relationships between records.

Stores:

  • Nodes (entities)
  • Relationships (edges)
  • Properties (attributes)

Example:

(Alice)

   │ FRIEND

   ▼

(Bob)

   │ WORKS_WITH

   ▼

(Charlie)

Instead of using JOINs, graph databases efficiently traverse relationships.

Examples:

  • Neo4j
  • Amazon Neptune
  • TigerGraph

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Extremely fast relationship queries
  • Natural representation of connected data
  • Flexible relationship modeling

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Social networks
  • Recommendation systems
  • Fraud detection
  • Knowledge graphs
  • Network topology

docs.title: SQL vs NoSQL Comparison
docs.text: SQL NoSQL Tables Key-Value, Document, Wide-Column, Graph Fixed schema Flexible schema Supports JOIN Usually avoids JOIN Strong ACID support Varies by database Vertical scaling Horizontal scaling Best for transactional systems Best for scalable, flexible systems

docs.title: Advantages of NoSQL
docs.text:
• Flexible schema
  • Easy horizontal scaling
  • High performance
  • Handles large datasets
  • High availability
  • Optimized for specific workloads

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Limited JOIN support
  • Data duplication may occur
  • Consistency model depends on the database
  • Query languages are not standardized

docs.title: Popular NoSQL Databases
docs.text: Type Examples Key-Value Redis, DynamoDB Document MongoDB, CouchDB, Firestore Wide-Column Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB Graph Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, TigerGraph

docs.title: Q1. What is a NoSQL database?
docs.text:
Answer

A NoSQL database stores data using non-relational models such as key-value pairs, documents, wide columns, or graphs. It is designed for flexibility, scalability, and high performance.

docs.title: Q2. What are the main types of NoSQL databases?
docs.text:
Answer

  1. Key-Value
  2. Document
  3. Graph

docs.title: Q3. Why is MongoDB called a document database?
docs.text:
Answer

Because it stores data as JSON/BSON documents grouped into collections. Each document is a self-contained object with a flexible schema and can contain nested objects and arrays.

docs.title: Q4. Why use Redis?
docs.text:
Answer

Redis is an in-memory key-value database optimized for extremely fast data access. It is commonly used for caching, session storage, and rate limiting.

docs.title: Q5. Why use a graph database?
docs.text:
Answer

Graph databases are optimized for querying relationships between entities, making them ideal for social networks, recommendation systems, fraud detection, and knowledge graphs.

docs.title: Q6. When should you choose NoSQL instead of SQL?
docs.text:
Answer

Choose NoSQL when your application requires flexible schemas, horizontal scalability, high throughput, or stores large amounts of semi-structured or connected data.

docs.title: What is a Relational Database?
docs.text:
A Relational Database (RDBMS) stores data in tables (relations).

Tables are connected using relationships such as:

  • Primary Key (PK)
  • Foreign Key (FK)

Examples:

  • MySQL
  • PostgreSQL
  • SQL Server
  • Oracle

docs.title: Why use a Relational Database?
docs.text:
Relational databases are best when:

  • Data has relationships.
  • Transactions must be reliable.
  • Data integrity is important.
  • Complex SQL queries and JOINs are required.
  • Strong consistency is required.

Examples:

  • Banking
  • E-commerce
  • Hospital systems
  • Student management systems

docs.title: What is a Transaction?
docs.text:
A transaction is a group of operations treated as one unit of work.

Example:

Bank transfer

Transfer $100

↓

Subtract $100 from Account A

↓

Add $100 to Account B

Both operations must succeed together.

docs.title: A — Atomicity
docs.text:
Definition

A transaction is all or nothing.

If one operation fails, the entire transaction is rolled back.

Example:

Transfer $100

Account A -100 ✅

Account B +100 ❌

↓

Rollback

Account A restored
Account B unchanged

No partial updates are allowed.

docs.title: C — Consistency
docs.text:
Definition

A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another while respecting all rules and constraints.

Examples of rules:

  • Primary key uniqueness
  • Foreign key constraints
  • CHECK constraints
  • NOT NULL constraints
  • Business rules

Example:

Orders.user_id = 999

↓

User 999 does not exist

↓

Transaction rejected ❌

The database remains consistent.

docs.title: I — Isolation
docs.text:
Definition

Multiple transactions can run at the same time, but they should not interfere with each other in a way that produces incorrect results.

Example:

Two ATMs withdraw money simultaneously.

Without isolation:

Balance = $100

ATM A reads $100

ATM B reads $100

ATM A withdraws $80

ATM B withdraws $80

Final balance = -$60 ❌

With proper isolation:

Balance = $100

ATM A withdraws $80

Balance = $20

ATM B checks balance

Insufficient funds

Transaction rejected

The database prevents incorrect concurrent behavior.

docs.title: D — Durability
docs.text:
Definition

Once a transaction is committed, its changes are permanent.

Even if the database crashes immediately afterward, the committed data is not lost.

Example:

Transfer committed ✅

↓

Power failure ⚡

↓

Restart database

↓

Money transfer still exists ✅

This is typically achieved using transaction logs (e.g., Write-Ahead Logging).

docs.title: ACID Summary
docs.text: Property Meaning Atomicity All operations succeed or all are rolled back. Consistency Data always satisfies rules and constraints. Isolation Concurrent transactions do not interfere incorrectly. Durability Committed changes survive crashes.

docs.title: Real Banking Example
docs.text:
Account A = $1000

Account B = $500

Transfer $200

↓

BEGIN

↓

A = 800

↓

B = 700

↓

COMMIT

If any step fails before COMMIT:

ROLLBACK

A = 1000

B = 500

docs.title: Why ACID is Important
docs.text:
Without ACID:

  • Money could disappear.
  • Inventory counts could become incorrect.
  • Duplicate orders could occur.
  • Data corruption could happen.

docs.title: Popular Relational Databases
docs.text:
• MySQL
  • PostgreSQL
  • Microsoft SQL Server
  • Oracle Database
  • MariaDB

docs.title: Q1. What is a Relational Database?
docs.text:
Answer

A relational database stores structured data in tables and uses relationships (primary keys and foreign keys) to connect data. It supports SQL and ACID transactions.

docs.title: Q2. Why use a Relational Database?
docs.text:
Answer

Because it provides strong consistency, supports complex queries and JOINs, maintains relationships between data, and guarantees reliable transactions.

docs.title: Q3. What is a transaction?
docs.text:
Answer

A transaction is a sequence of database operations treated as a single unit of work. It either completes successfully or is rolled back.

docs.title: Q4. What is Atomicity?
docs.text:
Answer

All operations in a transaction succeed together or none of them are applied.

docs.title: Q5. What is Consistency?
docs.text:
Answer

Every transaction must leave the database in a valid state by satisfying all constraints and business rules.

docs.title: Q6. What is Isolation?
docs.text:
Answer

Transactions can execute concurrently, but each transaction should behave as if it were running independently, according to the configured isolation level.

docs.title: Q7. What is Durability?
docs.text:
Answer

Once a transaction is committed, the data is permanently stored and survives crashes or power failures.

docs.title: Q8. Why is ACID important for banking?
docs.text:
Answer

Bank transfers involve multiple updates. ACID guarantees that either all updates succeed together or none of them are applied, preventing lost money or inconsistent account balances.

docs.title: REST
docs.text: Representational State Transfer — resources identified by URLs, manipulated through a fixed set of HTTP verbs.

docs.title: Resource modeling
docs.text:
• Nouns, not verbs: /orders/42, not /getOrder?id=42.
  • Nest to express ownership: /users/7/orders for a user's orders.
  • Avoid deep nesting beyond 2 levels — prefer top-level resources with filter query params: /orders?userId=7 over /users/7/orders/items/3/tags.

docs.title: HTTP verbs and status codes
docs.text: Verb Meaning Idempotent? GET Read Yes POST Create No PUT Replace Yes PATCH Partial update No (usually) DELETE Remove Yes Status Meaning 200 OK 201 Created 204 No Content (success, empty body) 400 Bad request (client error, malformed input) 401 Unauthenticated 403 Authenticated but not authorized 404 Resource doesn't exist 409 Conflict (e.g. duplicate, version mismatch) 429 Rate limited 500 Server error

docs.title: HATEOAS
docs.text:
Responses can include links to related actions/resources, so clients discover what's possible next instead of hardcoding URL construction:

{
  "id": 42,
  "status": "pending",
  "links": {
    "self": "/orders/42",
    "cancel": "/orders/42/cancel"
  }
}

In practice, most REST APIs skip full HATEOAS — it adds payload size and client complexity that's rarely worth it outside of specific hypermedia use cases.

Common mistake

Using 200 OK for everything and putting the real status in the JSON body ({"success": false}). This breaks HTTP caching, monitoring, and every standard HTTP client's error handling — use real status codes.

docs.title: Techniques to Improve Database Performance, Availability & Scalability
docs.text:
Modern systems often use multiple techniques together:

  • Database Indexing
  • Database Replication
  • Database Partitioning
  • Database Sharding

docs.title: What is an Index?
docs.text:
An index is a data structure that allows the database to locate rows quickly without scanning the entire table.

Think of it like the index of a book.

Without an index:

Book

Page 1
Page 2
Page 3
...
Page 500

To find "Database", you may need to scan many pages.

With an index:

Index

Database → Page 325
Networking → Page 180
Spring → Page 95

Go directly to the page.

docs.title: Database Example
docs.text:
Without index:

SELECT * FROM users
WHERE email='alice@gmail.com';

Database scans every row.

Row1

Row2

Row3

...

Row1000000

With index:

Email Index

↓

alice@gmail.com

↓

Row 589321

The lookup is much faster.

docs.title: Common Index Types
docs.text:
• B+ Tree (most common)
  • Hash Index
  • Full-text Index
  • Bitmap Index (specialized)

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Faster queries
  • Faster searching
  • Better sorting
  • Better JOIN performance

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Uses additional storage
  • Slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE because indexes must also be updated

docs.title: What is Replication?
docs.text:
Replication copies the same data from one database (Primary) to one or more replicas.

          Primary Database
                 |
      ---------------------
      |                   |
 Replica 1           Replica 2

All replicas contain the same data.

docs.title: High Availability
docs.text:
If the primary fails:

Primary ❌

↓

Replica promoted

↓

System continues working

docs.title: Read Scalability
docs.text:
Write operations go to the primary.

Read operations can go to replicas.

          Client

        Read Request

              ↓

 Replica A

 Replica B

 Replica C

This reduces load on the primary.

docs.title: Synchronous Replication
docs.text:
The primary waits until replicas confirm the write.

Advantages:

  • Strong consistency

Disadvantages:

  • Higher write latency

docs.title: Asynchronous Replication
docs.text:
The primary commits immediately.

Replicas update later.

Advantages:

  • Faster writes

Disadvantages:

  • Replication lag (temporary inconsistency)

docs.title: 3. Database Partitioning
docs.text:
Partitioning splits one large table into smaller logical partitions within the same database.

Example:

Orders table

Orders

↓

2023 Partition

2024 Partition

2025 Partition

Queries only search the relevant partition.

Example:

SELECT *

FROM Orders

WHERE order_year = 2025;

Only the 2025 partition is scanned.

docs.title: Types of Partitioning
docs.text:
• Range Partition
  • List Partition
  • Hash Partition

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Faster queries
  • Easier maintenance
  • Smaller indexes

docs.title: What is Sharding?
docs.text:
Sharding splits different data across multiple database servers.

Each shard owns a subset of the data.

Example:

Shard 1

Users 1 - 1,000,000

-----------------------

Shard 2

Users 1,000,001 - 2,000,000

-----------------------

Shard 3

Users 2,000,001 - 3,000,000

Unlike replication, shards do not contain the same data.

docs.title: Request Flow
docs.text:
Client

↓

Shard Router

↓

Shard 2

↓

User 1,500,000

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Massive horizontal scalability
  • Smaller databases
  • Higher write throughput

docs.title: Challenges
docs.text:
• Cross-shard JOINs are difficult
  • Rebalancing shards can be complex
  • More application logic

docs.title: Replication vs Sharding
docs.text: Replication Sharding Copies the same data Splits different data Improves availability Improves scalability Read scaling Read and write scaling Multiple copies Each shard owns unique data

docs.title: Combining Both
docs.text:
Large systems often use both.

                  Client
                     |
                Shard Router
              /             \
             /               \
        Shard A          Shard B
          |                 |
      ---------         ---------
      |       |         |       |
 Primary Replica     Primary Replica

Each shard stores different data, and each shard has its own replicas for high availability.

docs.title: Q1. What is a database index?
docs.text:
Answer

A database index is a data structure that speeds up data retrieval by allowing the database to locate rows without scanning the entire table.

docs.title: Q2. What are the disadvantages of indexes?
docs.text:
Answer

Indexes require extra storage and increase the cost of INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations because they must also be maintained.

docs.title: Q3. What is database replication?
docs.text:
Answer

Replication copies the same data from a primary database to one or more replicas to improve availability, fault tolerance, and read scalability.

docs.title: Q4. What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication?
docs.text:
Answer

  • Synchronous replication waits for replicas before committing.
  • Asynchronous replication commits immediately and updates replicas later.

docs.title: Q5. What is database partitioning?
docs.text:
Answer

Partitioning divides a large table into smaller logical partitions within the same database to improve query performance and maintenance.

docs.title: Q6. What is database sharding?
docs.text:
Answer

Sharding distributes different portions of data across multiple database servers, allowing the system to scale horizontally.

docs.title: Q7. What is the difference between partitioning and sharding?
docs.text:
Answer

Partitioning divides a table within a single database instance, while sharding distributes data across multiple independent database servers.

docs.title: Q8. What is the difference between replication and sharding?
docs.text:
Answer

Replication duplicates the same data to improve availability and read performance. Sharding splits different data across servers to improve storage capacity and write scalability.
